sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Dilemma
sections.description: The clinical narrative begins with a man in his 60s presenting to the emergency department with an acute constellation of symptoms that initially obscured the underlying etiology. His chief complaints included a three-day history of high-grade fever, severe headache, general malaise, and persistent hiccups, accompanied by arthralgia affecting the shoulders and ankles. While the fever and headache are non-specific indicators of infection or inflammation, the persistence of hiccups served as a crucial clinical clue pointing toward central nervous system irritation or metabolic derangement. sections.section_title: Pathophysiological Basis: Behçet's Disease and Neuro-Inflammation
sections.description: Behçet's disease (BD) is a chronic, relapsing, multisystem vasculitis characterized primarily by recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis, often accompanied by distinct skin lesions such as erythema nodosum or folliculitis-like rashes. While the disease affects multiple organ systems, neurological involvement—termed neuro-Behçet's disease (neuro-BD)—occurs in approximately 10% to 20% of patients. In the vast majority of cases, neuro-BD manifests as a delayed complication, appearing several years after the initial diagnosis of systemic BD. sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: Confirming SIADH and Excluding Mimics
sections.description: The confirmation of Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH) in this case relied on the rigorous application of biochemical criteria that distinguish true SIADH from other causes of hyponatremia. The patient presented with profound hyponatremia (124 mmol/L) and hypo-osmolar serum (267 mOsm/kg), yet his urine was inappropriately concentrated (900 mOsm/kg) with elevated urinary sodium (88 mmol/L). Crucially, the patient was clinically euvolemic, lacking signs of dehydration or edema, which rules out hypovolemic or hypervolemic etiologies. sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy: Colchicine Monotherapy in Acute Neuro-BD
sections.description: The management of acute neurological Behçet's disease (neuro-BD) traditionally relies on high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, often followed by aggressive immunosuppressive agents such as cyclophosphamide or azathioprine, particularly when parenchymal brainstem lesions are present. In this case, the patient presented with a complex clinical picture involving fever, headache, aseptic meningitis, and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). While the severity of neurological symptoms typically mandates immediate steroid intervention to prevent irreversible parenchymal damage, the treating team opted for colchicine monotherapy.
